根据标准曲线测定结果，经回归方程计算发现其分子量绝大部分分布在 5000 Da 以上；经酶解后阿胶溶液在保留时间 55.5 min 出现了新的峰，分子量为

16 Da，且分子量 5000 Da 以下的物质增多。结果表明，经过碱性蛋白酶的处理，阿胶大分子蛋白或多肽被进一步水解，分子量减小。阿胶分子质量的降低能够使其具有较好的溶解性，机体更容易消化吸收，从而提高了阿胶的生物利用度[29]。

# 2.4　抗氧化活性结果分析

2.4.1   阿胶酶解前后抗氧化活性　阿胶未酶解和酶解后的 ABTS+自由基清除率见图 4。阿胶未酶解和酶解后的 ABTS+自由基清除率的趋势相同。在浓度为 0~10 mg/mL 之间具有量效关系，且具有统计学显著差异（P<0.05）；ABTS+自由基清率随溶液浓度的增大逐渐升高；在浓度为 10 mg/mL 时，未酶解阿胶和酶解后的阿胶蛋白肽溶液清除 ABTS+自由基的能力达到最高，分别为 75.83%±0.32% 和 93.16%±0.21%。由图 4 可见，所有同等剂量下阿胶酶解液的ABTS+自由基清除率均高于未酶解的阿胶溶液，与樊雨梅等[30] 的结果一致。Oh 等[31] 的研究表明，产生这一结果的原因是蛋白原料的酶解产物对 ABTS+自由基的清除率与其蛋白原料中的酪氨酸、色氨酸、半胱氨酸、蛋氨酸等抗氧化氨基酸的含量高度相关。

图 4    酶解处理对阿胶蛋白肽的ABTS+自由基清除率的影响  
Fig.4    Effects of enzymatic hydrolysis on ABTS+ radical   
scavenging rate of donkey hide gelatin peptides   
![](images/8d44f096c9b6768fa6264238af294dc05b729f6b61fc12dadb880767076ca84f.jpg)  
注：不同字母表示同一酶解条件下数据差异显著，P<0.05；图5同。

未酶解阿胶溶液和酶解后阿胶蛋白肽的 DPPH自由基清除率见图 5。未酶解阿胶溶液清除 DPPH自由基的趋势呈先下降后上升的趋势，在阿胶溶液浓度为 2 mg/mL时，对 DPPH 自由基的清除率最高，为 16.93%±2.41%；在阿胶溶液浓度为 6 mg/mL，DPPH 自由基清除率最低，为 4.23%±1.74%；在溶液浓度 4~6 mg/mL 和 8~10 mg/mL 之间具有量效关系，且具有统计学显著性差异（P<0.05）。酶解后的阿胶蛋白肽对 DPPH自由基的清除率呈上升趋势，在溶液浓度为 10 mg/mL 时，对 DPPH 自由基的清除率最高，为 39.95%±1.27%；阿胶酶解液浓度在 2~4 mg/mL之间具有量效关系，且具有显著性差异（P<0.05）。所有同等剂量下酶解后阿胶蛋白肽溶液的 DPPH自由基清除率均高于未酶解的阿胶溶液，这与Wu等[32] 的结果一致。

![](images/9fc01b589ca9396598795717b184911dc5af9368c30532ab14f393a42d0e944a.jpg)  
图 5    酶解处理对阿胶蛋白肽的 DPPH自由基清除率的影响  
Fig.5    Effects of enzymatic hydrolysis on DPPH radical scavenging rate of donkey hide gelatin peptide

2.4.2   不同分子量阿胶蛋白肽抗氧化活性的测定结果　采用碱性蛋白酶酶解得到的阿胶蛋白肽，经过超滤技术将阿胶蛋白肽分离为>30 kDa、10~30 kDa、3~10 kDa、1~3 kDa 和<1 kDa 五个组分。不同组分阿胶蛋白肽 ABTS+清除率结果如图 6所示。随着阿胶蛋白肽浓度的增大，ABTS+自由基清除率也随之增大，其变化趋势与谷胱甘肽对 ABTS+自由基清除效果相似。从图 6 可以看出，阿胶蛋白肽以高浓度存在时，其抗氧化活性高。在 2~6 mg/mL浓度范围内，不同超滤组分的 ABTS+自由基清除率随阿胶蛋白肽浓度增加而显著（P<0.05）升高，在 6~10 mg/mL 浓度范围内，自由基清除率变化趋势不明显。在10 mg/mL 时不同分子量的阿胶蛋白肽清除能力最大，ABTS+自由基清除率由大到小依次为：分子量1~3 kDa，分子量 3~10 kDa，分子量>30 kDa，分子量<1 kDa，分子量 10~30 kDa。本研究中分子量 1~3 kDa的阿胶蛋白肽在 10 mg/mL 浓度下具有良好的抗氧化效果，且与其他分子量的阿胶蛋白肽相比差异显著（P<0.05）。郑天芝[33] 通过对茶渣抗氧化肽的研究，得出分子量 1~3 kDa 的茶渣抗氧化肽具有良好的抗氧化效果，与本研究的结论一致。

![](images/efb6f47a7fec6b7ef8b4829726b044194a193790d5d6141c6bb4e53754f96cd6.jpg)  
图 6    不同分子量阿胶蛋白肽的ABTS+自由基清除率  
Fig.6    ABTS+ radical scavenging rate of donkey hide gelatin peptides with different molecular weights

由图 7可知，不同组分阿胶蛋白肽的 DPPH自由基清除率随阿胶蛋白肽浓度的增加而增强，且与谷胱甘肽对 DPPH 自由基清除率的趋势大致相同，

在 2~10 mg/mL的浓度范围内具有一定的量效关系。当阿胶蛋白肽的浓度为 10 mg/mL 时，DPPH自由基清除率最强。其中<1 kDa的阿胶蛋白肽自由基清除率最高为 48.7±21.11%，其次为分子量 10~30 kDa（41.69%±3.84%），分子量 1~3 kDa（37.80%±1.37%），分子量>30 kDa（28.95%±2.89%）。结果表明，在一定浓度条件下，分子量的变化对阿胶蛋白肽清除 DPPH 自由基的清除能力有显著影响，且分子量越小清除能力越强。低分子量的阿胶蛋白肽倾向于与 DPPH 自由基反应，这可能会增加多肽或氨基酸小分子去除自由基的能力。相关研究表明，在一定浓度范围内，食源性肽的分子量越低，其抗氧化活性越强[34]。例如，王宝琴[35] 在对榛子抗氧化肽活性分析时发现，分子量最小的榛子抗氧化肽组分（<1 kDa）的 DPPH 自由基清除率最强。

![](images/d86b608ada74c265ab161d61be59ae62b3b960d1b5ff1c6758dbbce348dbdce6.jpg)  
图 7    不同分子量阿胶蛋白肽的DPPH自由基清除率  
Fig.7    DPPH radical scavenging rate of donkey hide gelatin peptides with different molecular weights

# 3 结论

本实验研究获得了阿胶蛋白肽的最佳酶解工艺，发现酶解后阿胶蛋白肽的抗氧化活性高于未酶解的阿胶，并且小分子的阿胶蛋白肽具有较强的ABTS+及 DPPH自由基清除率，说明阿胶蛋白肽具有良好的体外抗氧化活性。然而本研究未涉及阿胶蛋白肽体内抗氧化活性的检测及抗氧化机理的探讨，这也是今后需要解决的问题及研究方向。本实验研究为后续开展阿胶蛋白肽抗氧化机理探索奠定良好基础，也为阿胶新产品的开发提供一定的理论依据。

# 基于造血活性小肽研究阿胶炮制原理

付英杰1 , 司子林2 , 刘 月3 , 贾玉民4 , 陈 智5 , 陈小天1 , 王建安1∗

(1. 济宁医学院药学院, 山东 日照 276826; 2. 中国药科大学药学院, 江苏 南京 211198; 3. 江西中医药大学药学院, 江西 南昌 330103; 4. 东阿阿胶股份有限公司, 国家胶类中药工程技术研究中心, 山东东阿 252201; 5. 山东中医药大学药学院, 山东 济南 250355)

摘要: 目的 基于造血活性小肽研究阿胶炮制原理。 方法　 Orbitrap-MS 法对阿胶及其炮制品 (蛤粉炒、 蒲黄炒) 的酶解 超滤物进行数据解析 根据分值 丰度 韦恩图 热图聚类分析推断其可能具有造血活性或具有深入研究价值的肽序列 采用 固相合成法对其进行合成 检测纯度 三氟乙酸残留 净肽含量 内毒素等 以红细胞爆式集落形成单位为指标 检测阿胶及其炮制品的酶解 超滤物和 种合成肽活性 结果 共检测出 种肽 其中 个来源于胶原蛋白 蛤粉炒阿胶 种新肽产生 种肽消失 蒲黄炒阿胶 种新肽产生 种肽消失 多数肽序列保持不变, 但丰度有所改变。 以其中 13 种肽作为对象进行 Fmoc 合成, 发现其均可用于细胞培养。 结论 阿胶炮制后,造血活性升高, 推测是胶原蛋白裂解并经消化产生 ejp33 ( GVVGLPGQR) 强活性肽、 ejp131 ( GPAGPSGPPGKDGT)弱活 性 肽 以 达 到 增 效 作 用, 且 其 促 造 血 效 果 是 以 ejp10 ( GPAGPIGPV ) 、 ejp6 ( GPAGPTGPV ) 、 ejp77(LSSPARSGASL) 为主的数种肽的协同作用。

关键词: 阿胶; 蛤粉炒; 蒲黄炒; 酶解; Orbitrap-MS; 红细胞爆式集落形成单位; Fmoc 固相合成

# Processing principles of Asini Corii Colla based on hematopoietic small peptides

FU Ying-jie1, 　 SI Zi-lin2, 　 LIU Yue3, 　 JIA Yu-min4, 　 CHEN Zhi5, 　 CHEN Xiao-tian1,WANG Jian-an1∗

(1. College of Pharmacy, Jining Medical University, Rizhao 276826, China; 2. College of Pharmacy, China Pharmaceutical University, Nanjing 211198, China; 3. College of Pharmacy, Jiangxi University of Traditional Chinese Medicine, Nanchang 330103, China; 4. National Engineering Technology Research Center for Grum Traditional Chinese Medicine, Dong’ e Ejiao Co., Ltd., Dong’ e 252201, China; 5. College of Pharmacy, Shandong University of Traditional Chinese Medicine, Jinan 250355, China)

ABSTRACT: AIM 　 To study the processing principles of Asini Corii Colla based on small hematopoietic peptides. METHODS 　 The data of enzymolysis ultrafiltration products of Asini Corii Colla and its processed products ( stir-fried with clam powder or cattail) were analyzed by Orbitrap-MS method, and the peptide sequences that may have hematopoietic activity or have in-depth research value were predicted according to the result of score, abundance, Venn diagram and thermographic cluster analysis. The sythesized peptides using Fmoc solid-phase synthesis method had determinations of their purity and net content, residual trifluoroacetic acid, endotoxin, etc. The enzymolysis ultrafiltration products of Asini Corii Colla and its processed products, and the activities of thirteen synthetic peptides underwent detection with burst-forming unit-erythroid as an indicator. RESULTS　 Among the totally detected one hundred and seventy-one peptides, one hundred and twenty-seven were derivatives from collagen. Asini Corii Colla stir fried with clam powder was observed with twenty-six new peptides, and disappearance of, twenty-one peptides; Asini Corii Colla stir fried with cattail was observed with sixteen new peptides, and disappearance of fifty-two peptides; with most peptide sequences remained unchanged, but the

abundance changed. The thirteen peptides selected as targets for Fmoc synthesis can all be used for cell culture. CONCLUSION　 Processed Asini Corii Colla contributes improved hematopoietic activity. It is speculated that the degraded collagen produces strong active peptide ejp33 ( GVVGLPGQR ) and weak active peptide ejp131 (GPAGPSGPPGKDGT) to achieve synergistic effect; and ejp10 ( GPAGPIGPV) , ejp6 ( GPAGPTGPV) and ejp77 (LSSPARSGASL) being the major synergistically hematopoietic peptides.

KEY WORDS: Asini Corii Colla; stir-fried with clam powder; stir-fried with cattail; enzymolysis; Orbitrap-MS; burst-forming unit-erythroid; Fmoc solid-phase synthesis

阿胶炮制历史悠久, 相关研究主要集中在工艺改进上[1-2] 其炮制后大分子胶原蛋白裂解成较小的分子, 减少了胃肠消化负担, 因此降低了滋腻之性; 蛤粉烫后, 阿胶中钙离子增多而增强止血作用, 其他微量元素含量也有增加, 有助于其补益作用; 炮制后阿胶挥发性氨基氮大幅度减少或产生改变 对胃肠刺激减弱 炮制前后对氨基酸基本没有破坏[2-3]。 但对阿胶炮制后肽类成分的变化甚少提及, 仅发现酸解后没有新成分出现[4], 由于酸水解后低肽也被完全水解成氨基酸 表明氨基酸种类没有改变, 这也提示阿胶炮制机制研究可以完全排除氨基酸残基的变化, 只需从序列的改变入手。

2020 年版 《中国药典》 收载的阿胶规格为生品 蛤粉炒 蒲黄炒 炮制方法是先将蛤粉或蒲黄用中火炒至一定程度后 投入阿胶丁 炒至鼓起呈圆球形、 内无溏心时取出, 蛤粉炒偏于润肺燥, 蒲黄炒偏于止血[5]。 由此推测, 阿胶炮制后其大分子蛋白裂解成低分子肽 由于辅料不同 蛤粉蒲黄等) , 其裂解的方式可能不同, 并且裂解有一定规律性 阿胶及炮制品被肠吸收的部分除氨基酸外 还有多种小肽 可能具有较强的造血活性 为了验证该推测 本实验以阿胶经酶解得到的肽为基础 研究其炮制前后的序列变化 以期对阿胶造血物质基础和炮制机制进行深层次的探讨

# 2　 方法

样品制备 参考文献 报道制备蒲黄炒阿胶 蛤粉炒阿胶 称取阿胶 蒲黄炒阿胶 蛤粉炒阿胶各 水炖化后定容至 量瓶中, 依次加入胃蛋白酶0. 165 g ( pH=2) 、 胰-糜复合蛋白酶 0. 375 g ( pH= 8) 酶解 4 h, 95 ℃水浴灭活蛋白酶 滤过 得酶解液[7] 稀释至5 g / L, 设定操作压力为 (0. 15±0. 01) MPa, 酶解液温度为40 ℃ , 经 1 kDa 中空纤维超滤膜, 收集分子量 超滤液[7] 获得 种组

分 其中 为 阿胶超滤液 为kDa 阿胶超滤液, s3 为<1 kDa 蒲黄炒阿胶超滤液,s4 为 1 ~ 10 kDa 蒲黄炒阿胶超滤液, s5 为< 1 kDa蛤粉炒阿胶超滤液 为 蛤粉炒阿胶超滤液 在温度 压力 条件下蒸发至约11 mL, 在- 40 ℃下预冻 4 h 后冷冻真空干燥12 h, 即得[8] 。 取适量, 0. 1% 三氟乙酸复溶, $\mathrm { C } _ { 1 8 }$ SPE 固相萃取柱脱盐, 0. 1% 三氟乙酸清洗, 乙腈-水-三氟乙酸 (4 ∶ 1 ∶ 0. 005) 洗脱, 再进行冷冻真空干燥, 平行3 次。

# 2. 2　 样品分析

2. 2. 1　 色谱条件 参考文献 [ 9] 报道, RP-C液相色谱柱 ( 75 μm×150 mm, 1. 7 μm) ; 流动相0. 1% 甲酸 ( A) -84% 乙腈 ( B) , 梯度洗脱 ( 0 ~50 min，4%~50%B；50~54 min，50%~100%B;54 ~ 60 min, 100% B) ; 体积流量 200 nL / min; 柱温 40 ℃ ; 检测波长 280 nm; 进样量 20 μL。  
2. 2. 2　 质谱条件 参考文献 [10-11] 报道, 正离子模式; 母离子扫描范围 m / z 300 ~ 1 800; 一级质谱分辨率 m / z 为 时 多肽及其碎片的质量电荷比方法为每次全扫描后采集 个碎片图谱 (MS2 碰撞池) ; 隔离窗口 m / z 1. 6; 二级质谱分辨率 碰撞能量  
数据库检索 采用 软件进行处理 相关参数为肽相对分子质量容差 ×-5 容差 胰蛋白酶 最大不完全酶解位点数目 固定修饰半胱氨酸碘乙酰胺可变修饰氧化 ( M) ; 数据库选用 uniprot _ Equus(马属动物) _ 47783_ 20190501+NCBI_ Equus_asinus（马属动物驴）_43166_20190507；结果过滤参数 FDR≤0. 01[12-13] 。

# 小肽化学合成

第 个氨基酸缩合 称取为肽链 端第 个氨基酸 适量 在 下溶于干燥二氯甲烷中 加入 N N 二异丙基碳二亚胺在 下搅拌 如有沉淀则加入二甲基甲酰胺至溶解 将溶液加到处理好的王氏树脂中 加入溶于二甲基甲酰胺的 二甲氨基吡啶搅拌 依次用二甲基甲酰胺、 二氯甲烷各清洗3 次, 茚三酮反应检测氨基酸与树脂的缩合程度, 若不变色则结束反应 在二甲基甲酰胺中加入乙酸酐 吡啶以覆盖剩余羟基 搅拌 封闭后滤出溶液, 向反应容器中加入适量二甲基甲酰胺洗涤树脂 反应器 静置 后过滤除去溶剂 重复

次 依次用甲醇 二氯甲烷 二甲基甲酰胺各洗涤1 次。

2. 3. 2　 Nα Fmoc 保护去除 二甲基甲酰胺-哌啶(8 ∶ 2) 混合液填充多肽固相合成反应容器至 2 / 3,搅拌 滤过 向反应容器中加入适量二甲基甲酰胺洗涤树脂、 反应器, 静置10 s, 滤过, 重复2 次, 依次用甲醇、 二氯甲烷、 二甲基甲酰胺各洗涤 1 次。  
所有氨基酸连接 当树脂与第 个氨基酸耦合之后 其余氨基酸以目标肽从 端到 端的顺序, 依次按 2. 3. 1” 项下方法缩合[14-15] 。  
三氟乙酸裂解 称取合成后树脂 加入二氯甲烷使其膨胀, 每 100 mg 树脂加入 10 mL 裂解液 [三 氟 乙 酸-水-三 异 丙 基 硅 烷 ( 95 ∶ 2. 5 ∶搅拌裂解 砂芯过滤装置过滤滞留在砂芯上的树脂用新鲜裂解液清洗 次 回收滤液, 在真空条件下浓缩至原体积的1 / 4, 加入 10倍量甲基叔丁醚, 剧烈搅拌使肽沉淀, 洗涤过滤,重复 次 将沉淀肽溶于乙腈 水 三氟乙酸50 ∶ 0. 1) 混合溶液中并冻干。  
三氟乙酸去除 当三氟乙酸质量分数 %时 会对体外细胞培养实验产生明显影响[15] 故需将其去除 在冻干过程中 三氟乙酸大部分被去除, 而残存的采用成盐形式, 通过离子交换法柱 进行分离

# 2. 4　 合成品检测

2. 4. 1　 色谱条件　 Inertsil ODS-3 色谱柱 (4. 6 mm×流动相水 含 % 三氟乙酸乙腈 含 %三氟乙酸 梯度洗脱min，5% ~65% B：25~32 min，95% B：32~ 40min, 5% B) ; 体积流量 1 mL / min; 柱温20 ℃ ; 检测波长 220 nm; 进样量 5 μL。  
质谱条件 电喷雾 离子源 雾化气体积流量1. 5 L / min; 干燥气体积流量 5 L / min;装置温度 加热块温度 液相体积流量 0. 2 mL / min; 进样量 0. 3 μL。  
三氟乙酸残留分析 取 样品溶于纯水中 加水稀释至 采用去除三氟乙酸时所用 柱对其离子进行分离 得离子色谱 设定色谱条件为 色谱柱 进样量再制备 三氟乙酸标准液 以其质量浓度为横坐标 X 保留时间为纵坐标 Y绘制标准曲线, 计算该成分残留量[16]。  
内毒素测定 采用鲎试剂法[17]进行测定

净肽含量测定 通过微量有机元素分析仪测定合成肽中 N 含量[18], 计算净肽含量, 公式为净肽含量=元素测定含氮量×肽理论分子质量/ (肽链中 N 数量×N 相对原子质量)。  
溶解度测定 对合成肽用不同溶液进行溶解度测定, 以≥0. 1 mg / mL 为可溶。  
2. 5　 酶解超滤物冻干粉红细胞爆式集落形成单位测定  
2. 5. 1　 培养基配制 采用加入甲基纤维素的改良培养基 可使细胞更易悬浮生长 配方为马血清250 mL / L、 2-巯基乙醇 1. 0×10-4 mol / L、 rHuEpo 2U / mL、 IL-3 溶液 2 ng / mL、 青链霉素 100 U / mL、甲基纤维素 (终质量浓度 0. 9% ) 、 1640 或 IMDM培养基补足[19]  
样品配制 按照提取率折算 样品冻干粉与阿胶原药材酶解纯化液的比例为 1 μg / mL ∶ 6. 25mg / mL。 预实验发现, 20 μg / mL 细胞的培养效果较佳 即蛤粉炒阿胶 蒲黄炒阿胶含量均折合为125 mg / mL。  
培养方法 脱颈椎法处死大鼠 浸泡在%乙醇中 持续时间少于 剪去多余肌肉 取出股骨 置于 中浸泡后转移至 % 乙醇中浸泡1 min, 取出, 刮去组织残肉, 剪断两端,用马血清+1640 培养基混合液10 mL 冲出细胞, 吹打混匀[20-21] , 吸取 10 μL 至 EP 管中, 再吸取 180μL 马血清+1640 培养基混合液混匀, 计数, 稀释至细胞密度为 × 5 培养于 孔板上 每孔加入 细胞液 培养基 使最终细胞密度为 $1 \times 1 0 ^ { 5 } / \mathrm { m L }$ , 在 37 ℃ , 5% CO 条件下培养7 d[22]。 计数时, 以≥50 个细胞为1 个集落统计红细胞爆式集落形成单位  
种合成肽红细胞爆式集落形成单位的测定样品处理 加入超纯水制成质量浓度为的母液 使用前再用超纯水依次稀释至1 000、 100、 10 μg / mL, 0. 22 μm 微孔滤膜过滤。  
阳性对照药制备 将 用二甲基亚砜 溶解 制成质量浓度为的母液 临用前用超纯水稀释 即得溶液 称取 司坦唑醇 溶于 无水乙醇中, 制成质量浓度为 100 mg / mL 的母液,加入超纯水稀释成 % 无水乙醇稀释液 现配临用前用超纯水稀释 即得司坦唑醇溶液 按“2. 5” 项下方法进行细胞培养, 持续 4 d, 以≥25个细胞为 个集落 统计红细胞爆式集落形成

单位。

# 3　 结果

3. 1　 Obitrap-MS 分析 总离子流图谱见图 1, 二级质谱图见图2, 共获得 187 个肽序列, 以分子质量从小到大排序命名为 ejp1 ~ ejp187, 筛去重复及分值低于20 的肽序列及样品制备过程中使用的蛋白酶片段序列 ( ejp95、 137、 185 ~ 186) , 剩余 171个中有 42 个丰度为 0, 其原因可能是含量很低,或峰分离度不佳而无法提取峰面积。

为了比较生品、 蛤粉炒阿胶、 蒲黄炒阿胶间肽的区别, 将每组样品小于或大于1 kDa 的丰度进行合并, 通过 Venny 2. 1 软件绘制韦恩图, 见图 3,去除丰度为0 后, 对剩余129 个肽序列再进行丰度正态标准化, 采用 MEV 软件绘制热图, 见图 4,热图聚类后, 再结合以阿胶生品为对照的丰度, 计算 种炮制品比率 并进行分类 结果 个肽序列中 127 个来源于胶原蛋白, 占总量的 74. 3% 。由图 3 可知, 阿胶炮制后 17 种肽消失, 其中来自于胶 原 蛋 白 的 肽 有 ejp86 ( AGPAGPAGPIGPV ) 、ejp87(ARGAPGPQGPR)、ejp93 (GAVGPRGPSGPQ)、ejp125(GERGFPGLPGPS)、ejp60(GPAGPAGPPGPI)、ejp25(GPAGPRGEP )、ejp16 ( GPAGPSGPPG)、ejp134( GPPGAPGAPGAPGPV )、 ejp30 ( GPSGPQGVR )、ejp162( GPTGEPGKPGDKGH)、 ejp17 ( PMGPSGPR)、ejp57 ( PSGPAGPTGAR )、 ejp171 ( SGLDGAKGDAGPAGPK ), 属 于 非 胶 原 蛋 白 类 的 有 ejp132(NLPLPPPPPPR)、 ejp177 ( GIPLPNFRIYYK)、 ejp152( SPTRSSAAPDPGPA )、 ejp138 ( SSGSTSGQQPLSP );蒲黄 炒 阿 胶 后 新 增 16 种 肽, 分 别 为 ejp103、ejp11、 ejp119、 ejp135、 ejp148、 ejp151、 ejp161、ejp29、 ejp45、 ejp50、 ejp56、 ejp65、 ejp68、ejp131、 ejp33、 ejp90, 除 了 ejp45 ( EPPLPQEK )为 遗 传 抑 制 因 子 片 段, ejp161为 非 胶 原 蛋 白 类domain 片段外, 其余 14 种均来自于胶原蛋白; 蛤粉炒阿胶后新增 26 种肽, 分别为 ejp117、 ejp12、ejp131、 ejp143、 ejp164、 ejp166、 ejp175、 ejp20、ejp31、 ejp33、 ejp34、 ejp35、 ejp4、 ejp48、 ejp5、ejp55、 ejp7、 ejp70、 ejp72、 ejp73、 ejp76、 ejp81、ejp88、 ejp90、 ejp91、 ejp84, 其中属于非胶原蛋白类 的 有 ejp117 ( AAGASAPGPAGGRP ) 、 ejp73( ESEDGKLPR ) 、 ejp4 ( PGATAPGR ) 、 ejp166(PGSTALSACSLER) 、 ejp5 ( VGSPGAPR) 、 ejp164（Decorin）、ejp91（PGSPAGLGKAHS），其余19 种

来自胶原蛋白 新增肽中属非胶原蛋白类的肽有种, 可能是来自于辅料, 或者胶原蛋白自身产生了变化; 蒲黄、 蛤粉炮制后共同出现的肽有3 种, 分别 为 ejp90 ( GFPGADGVAGPK ) 、 ejp33( GVVGLPGQR ) 、 ejp131 ( GPAGPSGPPGKDGT ) ,均来源于胶原蛋白 表明阿胶加热后有部分胶原蛋白可能存在固定的裂解模式 对于分子量小于kDa 的部分, 蛤粉炒后 18 种肽消失, 新增 15 种肽, 无变化的达 61 种, 而对于分子量大于 1 kDa的部分 蒲黄炒后 种肽消失 新增 种肽 无变化的达 种 蛤粉炒后 种肽消失 新增 种肽 无变化的达 种 另外 除了蒲黄炒后分子量小于1 kDa 的结果得不到合理解释外, 其他结果均表明阿胶炮制后大多数肽序列保持不变 对其炮制机制的研究应是产生变化的部分

图4 显示, 阿胶炮制后低肽丰度聚为9 类; 蛤粉炒后16 种肽含量升高, 95 种无明显变化, 19 种降低 而蒲黄炒后 种肽含量升高 种无明显变化, 88 种降低, 表明蛤粉炒对阿胶原有成分影响相对较小, 而蒲黄炒影响较大, 其中 ejp131 含量在2 种方法炒制后均升高, 虽然 ejp58 含量在比率数值上也是如此 但其来源为丝氨酸蛋白酶 而且在热图上变化不明显; ejp90 蒲黄炒及 ejp33 蒲黄炒 蛤粉炒丰度均为 并且均在定性中被检测到 根据其蛋白来源名 可能具有动物水平上的造血活性。 另外, 由于部分肽丰度较低, 故本实验 选 择 丰 度 较 高 者 进 行 合 成, 包 括 ejp10、ejp106、 ejp23、 ejp28、 ejp77、 ejp105、 ejp6、 ejp126。3. 2　 Fmoc 固相合成肽检测 结果见表 1。 由于相关数据过多, 故以 ejp131 ( GPAGPSGPPGKDGT)为代表, 设定样品质量浓度为 1 mg / mL, 鲎试剂检测灵敏度为 测得内毒素水平小于 10 EU / mg, 见表 2, 纯度检测色谱图见图检测结果见图 峰表 纯度见表 另

# 4　 讨论

结合 丰度 相对定量 来看 活性最高 但在蒲黄炒和蛤粉炒中无法定量 原因可能是色谱峰无法分开或含量低 推测它可能是蒲黄或蛤粉炒后增效的关键肽。 ejp131、 ejp33 均为炮制后产 生 的 肽, 并 均 来 自 于 马 属 动 物 驴 (Equusasinus) 的胶原蛋白, ejp131 丰度较高, 但仅在质量浓度为1 000 μg / mL 时有活性, 表明其仅可作为炮制后产生的指标性肽。 ejp10 活性仅次于 ejp33,且其在阿胶及其炮制品中的丰度相当高, 认为是阿胶及其炮制品中有效造血成分小肽之一。 此外, 在ejp23、 ejp6 的视野中随处可见巨噬细胞, 提示这 2种肽能够促进巨噬细胞的分化 可能是阿胶提升免疫作用 滋阴功效 的物质基础 表明蛤粉炒后ejp6、 ejp77、 ejp23, 蒲黄炒后 ejp10、 ejp6、 ejp77、分别是 存性 保留造血活性但含量降低的肽 推测阿胶炮制后 胶原蛋白裂解并经消化产生 强活性肽以达到增效作用

活性较好的几种肽存在共性 均来自于驴胶原蛋白 表明其裂解产物具有确定的造血活性 几种活性较好且丰度高的胶原蛋白肽 ( ejp10、 ejp6、其一级序列还具有明显的相似之处 氨基端均为 并且大多具有 的循环片段 (如 ejp33)。

但在红细胞爆式集落形成单位计数发现 单一成分的活性最高仅约为酶解超滤液的 % 且集

落细胞数也难以达到 个 个样品无法进行对比 因此标准下降为 个 提示阿胶及炮制品的促造血效果应为数种肽的协同作用 而并非单一的活 性 肽 起 效。 而 ejp10、 ejp6、 ejp77、 ejp23、等肽在炮制前后均存在 是起协同作用的共性物质基础, 其中前三者为主要活性成分。

蛤粉炒阿胶组与生阿胶组差异非常显著, 打破了传统上认为 “阿胶炮制后仅为肽段断裂, 降低滋腻之性 的看法[23] 蛤粉炒阿胶与生阿胶均进行了酶解 因此理论上如果仅为肽段断裂 其补血效果应该相近; 但实际其补血作用显著优于未炮制阿胶组 表明蛤粉炒阿胶中有新的升血成分产生其次, 与生阿胶组比较, 蒲黄炒阿胶具有显著的补血功效 而非传统意义上认为蒲黄炒偏止血 雷公炮炙论 [24] 云 凡使 先于猪脂内浸一宿 至明出 于柳木火上炙 待泡了 细碾用 表明阿胶自古以来多使用炮制品 炙后发泡即阿胶珠以增强补血之功 与今人多直接使用生品不同[25]本实验也证明了无论采用何种辅料炒制 阿胶的补血作用均被显著增强 因此临床上补血应提倡使用阿胶炮制品

阳性对照药 具有明确的升血作用但并非成品药物[26] 阳性对照药司坦唑醇为目前临床治疗再生障碍性贫血非重型使用的雄激素类药[27]。目前尚无文献报道具有明确升血作用并具成药性的

单一肽作为阳性对照 种阳性对照药剂量浓度均较小, 若按照样品浓度会产生大量沉淀影响观测,尚无与样品结构性质近似的阳性对照药可供选择。本实验目的旨在探讨炮制机制 成药性不作为主要考察指标 因此图 的重点是进行样品间相对药效的比较

文献 [22] 报道, 细胞培养7 d 后结果较培养4 d 后差, 原因是在第 4 天营养物质不足必须换液,而骨髓的造血干细胞多数难以贴壁, 所以换液后造成损失。 本实验发现, 将7 d 更换为 4 d 时减少了实验时间, 并且结果更优。

# Structural Characteristics and Antioxidant Mechanism of Donkey-Hide Gelatin Peptides by Molecular Dynamics Simulation

Rong Liang, Le Xu, Chen Fan, Lele Cao and Xingfeng Guo *

Agricultural Science and Engineering School, Liaocheng University, Liaocheng 252059, China; liangrong8209@163.com (R.L.); xule@lcu.edu.cn (L.X.); fanchen7810@126.com (C.F.); 18846170635@163.com (L.C.) * Correspondence: guoxingfeng@lcu.edu.cn

Abstract: This study aimed to explore the structural characteristics and antioxidant mechanism of donkey-hide gelatin peptides. After hydrolysis and ultrafiltration treatment, five gelatin peptides with different molecular weights (MWs) were obtained. Amino acid analysis showed that gelatin peptides with different MWs contained a large number of amino acids, including G, P, E, N, A, and R, and differences were noted in the content of various amino acids. Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy and circular dichroism revealed that these gelatin peptides differed in terms of the peak strength of functional groups and number of secondary structures. Moreover, 26 pentapeptides/hexapeptides were identified. Among them, we investigated by molecular docking how PGPAP, which has the best antioxidant activity, may interact with the Keap1 protein. The results showed that the PGPAP-Keap1 complex had a stable conformation, and Arg415, Gly462, Phe478, and Tyr572 were the key residues involved in the binding of the peptide PGPAP to Keap1. Our results demonstrated that PGPAP could serve as a bioactive peptide with antioxidant activity.

Keywords: gelatin peptides; antioxidant activity; structural characteristics; Keap1 protein; molecular dynamics simulations

# 1. Introduction

Free radicals in the body can react with biologically active molecules to cause cell or tissue damage. Oxidative stress is linked to many diseases, such as inflammation and depression. Some synthetic antioxidants can scavenge free radicals and prevent food from spoiling. Although synthetic antioxidants possess strong antioxidant activity, they may cause potential harm and toxicity, which limit application in food products [1]. Therefore, the development of healthy and natural antioxidants has become a research trend. Some recent studies have demonstrated that many animal and plant protein hydrolysates have good antioxidant activities [2]. In general, an active antioxidant peptide is composed of 3–16 amino acid residues. Antioxidant peptides have the ability to scavenge free radicals, inhibit lipid peroxidation, supply hydrogen, and chelate metal ions. Considering that foodborne antioxidant peptides are safe and nontoxic, research on antioxidant peptides has gradually become a hot topic.

Gelatin is a colloidal protein extracted from the collagen of animal bones, hides, tendons, and other connective tissues. It is a straight chain polymer formed by crosslinking 18 amino acids and peptides [3]. Currently, gelatin is used as a frozen food improver, confectionery additive, beverage clarifying agent, meat product improver, dairy product additive, food coating material, and sugar coating agent in the food industry [4]. Peptides derived from gelatin possess strong antioxidant properties. For example, the EC50 values of DPPH, OH, and $\overset { \cdot } { \mathrm { O } ^ { 2 - } }$ free radicals cleared by the skin gelatin hydrolysates of bluefin leatherjacket (Navodon septentrionalis) were 5.227, 1.147, and 4.752 mg/mL, respectively [5].

Moreover, after enzymatic hydrolysis via Protamex, these hydrolysates could scavenge DPPH free radicals and chelate $\mathrm { F e } ^ { \tilde { 2 } + }$ ions, confirming their antioxidant effects [6].

Extensive research has proven that the antioxidant activity of peptides is affected by various physicochemical properties, including the molecular weight (MW) of peptides as well as the type and sequence of amino acids [7]. Zhang et al. revealed that the MW distribution of peanut polypeptides with the best antioxidant activity was mainly observed below 1400 Da [8]. Liu et al. obtained whey protein antioxidant peptides with different MWs and found that the peptide group with the smallest MW (<10 kDa) had the strongest antioxidant activity [9]. Sun et al. hydrolyzed porcine hemoglobin using pepsin and obtained four groups of antioxidant peptides; they revealed that that the peptide group with a MW of <3 kDa had the strongest superoxide anion scavenging ability and lipid peroxidation inhibition ability [10]. In addition, amino acid composition is a factor affecting the bioactivity of antioxidant polypeptide molecules. The enzymatic hydrolysate of smooth hound (Mustelus mustelus) muscle protein with strong antioxidant activity contained a high proportion of highly active amino acids, including Leu, His, Tyr, and Met [11]. Moreover, antioxidant peptides require a certain spatial structure to exert their antioxidant effects. According to a previous study, the activity of antioxidant peptides with a certain spatial structure was higher than that of amino acid mixtures with the same mass ratio [12]. However, the relationship between the bioactivity and structure of antioxidant peptides as well as the interaction between the active sites of peptide chain and amino acid residues remain unclear. Exploring the structure–activity relationship of antioxidant peptides not only helps predict the antioxidant activity of polypeptides but also provides a theoretical reference for subsequent efficient screening and synthesis of highly bioactive peptides.

Another important aspect in studying antioxidant peptides is to reveal the antioxidant mechanism. In particular, molecular docking has gradually become an important approach to screen peptides and explore their antioxidant mechanism. It is well-known that the Keap1-Nrf2 pathway is important for human cells to cope with oxidative stress. Under oxidative stress, the body can activate this pathway to promote the expression of a series of endogenous antioxidant proteins, thereby improving the body’s antioxidant capacity to resist oxidative stress [13]. Many scholars have used this pathway combined with molecular docking to explore the peptides’ antioxidant mechanism. Li et al. screened 20 small peptides with potential antioxidant activity using molecular docking, among which DKK and DDW showed the strongest ability to dock and bind to Keap1 proteins [14]. Agrawal et al. successfully isolated and purified two peptides from millet protein hydrolysates, namely, TSSSLNMAVRGGLTR and STTVGLGISMRSASVR [15]. Molecular docking studies have shown that interactions between Ser/Thr residues and free radicals are the main source of antioxidant activity of the two peptides. Tonolo et al. extracted and identified 23 peptides from fermented milk protein, among which NTVPAKSCQAQPTTM, QGPIVLNPWDQVKR, and APSFSDIPNPIGSENSE showed a strong ability to dock and bind to Keap1 [16]. These three peptides have certain inhibitory effects on Keap1-Nrf2 PPI; moreover, they can upregulate the expression level and activity of antioxidant enzymes by activating the Keap1-Nrf2 pathway [17]. These studies provide a significant reference for exploring the antioxidant mechanism of active peptides.

This study aimed to explore the structure–activity relationship of donkey-hide gelatin peptides using amino acid analysis, Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, and circular dichroism (CD). In addition, gelatin peptides were identified, and the antioxidant peptides with a known sequence were synthesized. The antioxidant activity of gelatin peptides was analyzed, and the most active peptides were docked to the Keap1 protein through molecular docking. Moreover, the stability of the peptide–Keap1 complex was verified using molecular dynamic (MD) simulations to explore its antioxidant mechanism. This research may indicate the molecular mechanism of active peptides and provide a reference for application of gelatin peptides.

# 2.2. Amino Acid Composition of Gelatin Peptides with Different MWs

The antioxidant activity of peptides is closely related to their structural properties, such as MW, amino acid composition, and peptide configuration. To explore the structure–activity relationship, the amino acid composition, functional groups, and secondary structure of polypeptides with different MWs were detected and analyzed. The amino acid composition (a total of 17 amino acids) of each polypeptide group was analyzed (Table 1). Many amino acids, such as G, P, E, N, A, and R, were identified in each group of peptide hydrolysates. In addition, each group contained a certain amount of M, C, and H. The amino acid composition of a peptide has a crucial effect on its antioxidant activity, and some amino acids may be detected in the active sites of antioxidant peptides [19]. A previous study revealed that the E-L sequence contributed significantly to the free radical scavenging ability of the short antioxidant peptide YFYPEL [20,21]. Chi et al. (2015) reported that YLMSR and VLYEE had higher antioxidant activity than MILMR, which might be related to the presence of Y [22]. Saito et al. revealed that peptides containing Y had stronger antioxidant activity than those containing H; moreover, peptides containing W or Y at the carboxyl terminal showed stronger free radical scavenging ability [23]. In this study, although the amino acid types were identical among the peptide groups, differences were noted in the contents of various amino acids. For example, the contents of most of the amino acids (e.g., N and E) in the group with a MW of >30 kDa were higher because the overall amino acid content was higher in this group of large proteins, which are not completely hydrolyzed. However, the contents of G and I were the highest in peptides with a MW of 1–3 kDa. The difference in amino acid composition among different groups may be responsible for their different antioxidant activities.

# 2.3. Functional Groups and Secondary Structures of Gelatin Peptides with Different MWs

As shown in Figure 2, all gelatin peptides with different MWs showed absorbance in N–H $( 3 5 0 0 { - } 3 3 0 0 ~ \mathrm { { c m } ^ { - 1 } ) }$ , O–H $( 3 3 0 0 { - } 2 5 0 0 ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } )$ , unsaturated $\mathrm { C - H } \ ( > 3 0 0 0 \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } )$ , saturated $\mathrm { C - H } ( 3 0 0 0 0 { - } 2 8 0 0 \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } ) , { - } \mathrm { C = O } ( 1 8 5 0 { - } 1 6 0 0 \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } )$ , amide $( 1 7 0 0 - 1 6 0 0 ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } ) , \mathrm { C } \mathrm { = C }$ $( 1 6 8 0 - 1 6 2 0 \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } ) , \mathsf { C - N } \left( 1 3 6 0 - 1 1 8 0 \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } \right) , \mathsf { C - O } \left( 1 3 0 0 - 1 0 8 0 \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } \right) , \mathsf { S = O } \left( 1 2 2 0 - 1 0 4 0 \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } \right)$ , $\mathrm { C - O - C } ( 1 1 5 0 { \mathrm { - } } 9 0 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } )$ , $\mathrm { a n d - N O } _ { 2 } ( 1 6 0 0 { - } 1 5 0 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } )$ bands. Some of these bonds were found in amino acids, while some do not exist in amino acids such as S=O and –NO , which may produce absorption peaks due to stretching between amino acids. Gelatin peptides possessed the same absorption bands because they came from the same source and had the same amino acid composition. However, the peak strength of functional groups varied in peptide groups with different MWs (Figure 2a). This finding may be related to the different amino acid contents, indicating that the spatial structure of the polypeptide aqueous solution is different. It is certain that antioxidant peptides require a spatial structure to exert their antioxidant effects. Differences in spatial structure can affect the exposure of certain active groups and thus affect the antioxidant activity of polypeptides [12].

All CD spectra of gelatin peptides with different MWs showed a negative peak at approximately 200 nm, which is considered a p–p band (Figure 3a). In addition, a small positive band was observed at approximately 225 nm. Based on the CD spectra, polyproline II helix and random coil conformations were detected, with different ellipticity values at wavelengths below 220 nm indicating different content of conformations [24]. As shown in Figure 3b, gelatin peptides presented a high content of antiparallel conformations, followed by beta-turn, whereas random coil, parallel, and alpha-helix conformations were relatively rare. Although gelatin peptides with different MWs showed similar trends in the content of different secondary structures, some differences were also noted. These subtle differences can affect the antioxidant activity. For example, a small change in random coil conformation can influence the antioxidant activity [25]. Antioxidant peptides require a certain spatial structure to exert their antioxidant effects. The best free radical scavenging ability can be achieved when some special groups associated with antioxidant activity are fully exposed [26]. There may be some oligopeptides in gelatin peptides solution, which could not form secondary conformations alone, but some oligopeptides with a very short length may exist in the form of peptide complexes to exhibit a secondary structure [27]. Therefore, differences in the secondary structure of gelatin peptides is another factor affecting antioxidant activities.

# 2.6. Molecular Mechanism Analysis of Peptide PGPAP Binding to Keap1

Variations in the number of hydrogen bonds between the Keap1 protein and PGPAP polypeptide were analyzed (Figure 4e). The number of hydrogen bonds between them decreased slightly when the whole PGPAP–Keap1 complex underwent conformational change and stabilized, and the number of hydrogen bonds increased further. The average number of hydrogen bonds between Keap1 and PGPAP was 5.36 when the RMSD value was stable at 25–50 ns. Consequently, PGPAP polypeptide molecules could stably bind to Keap1 protein.

This study extracted the complex conformation of polypeptides after MD simulation and analyzed the interaction among them to confirm the main interaction regions between Keap1 and PGPAP as well as key amino acids involved in the interaction. As shown in Figure 5a, the polypeptide molecules are primarily bound to the hydrophobic cavities of the Keap1 protein. Based on the analysis shown in Figure 5b,c, the O atom (carboxyl oxygen from amide bond of the peptide PGPAP), which acts as the hydrogen bond acceptor formed a hydrogen bond with the surrounding amino acids like Arg415 and Gly462. Meanwhile, the polypeptide molecule also formed a π–π stacking interaction with the benzene ring on the surrounding amino acids—Phe478 and Tyr572—which further enhanced the affinity of the polypeptide molecule towards the Keap1 protein. The results indicated that the peptide PGPAP can stably bind to the active cavity of the Keap1 protein to play the corresponding biological role. In addition, the hydrophobic interfaces between PGPAP and Keap1 are shown in Figure 5d. The peptide PGPAP was bent and folded into the hydrophobic pocket of Keap1. The residues Gly462 and Phe478 were responsible for forming the PGPAPinduced hydrophobic interface, which helped the polypeptide molecules enter the active pocket and stably bind to the Keap1 protein.

The human Keap1 protein has five domains, namely, N-terminal region, POZ region (also known as the BTB region), IVR region, KELCH region, and C-terminal region [31]. The human Nrf2 protein can be divided into six conserved domains, namely, Neh1, Neh2, Neh3, Neh4, Neh5, and Neh6 [32]. The Neh2 region is responsible for binding to the Keap1 protein. Under normal physiological conditions, Nrf2 is continuously produced in cells. Keap1 binds to cytoplasmic actin through its POZ region to form homologous dimers; moreover, it binds to the DLG and ETGE sequences of the Neh2 region of Nrf2 protein through two Klech regions of the dimer [33]. In addition, the Keap1 protein dimer binds to Cul3 through its POZ region, which may promote the ubiquitination of the Nrf2 bound to the Keap1 protein dimer, thereby leading to the degradation of ubiquitinated Nrf2 and ensuring that free Nrf2 proteins in the body are present at low levels [34]. When the cells are under oxidative stress, foreign oxidants can alter the conformation of key cysteine residues in POZ and IVR regions of Keap1, thereby altering the conformation of the Keap1 dimer. This conformational change may interfere with the Keap1–Nrf2 interaction. If foreign antioxidants affect the Keap1–Nrf2 interaction, which may increase the intracellular Nrf2 content, then such substances can activate the pathway and improve the antioxidant capacity of the body. In this study, MD simulation suggested that PGPAP could stably bind

to Keap1, indicating that it has good potential antioxidant function. Further experiments are warranted to explore its intracellular antioxidant activity and mechanism using HepG2experiments are warranted to explore its intracellular antioxidant activity and mechanism cell models.using HepG

# 3. Materials and Methods

# 3.1. Materials and Reagents

Donkey-hide gelatin (batch number: 2110014) was purchased from Dong-E-E-Jiao $\mathrm { C o . , I }$ Ltd. (Liaocheng, China). Alcalase 2.4L was obtained from Novozymes Biotech. $C 0 . _ { }$ , Ltd. (CPH, Denmark). Potassium bromide (KBr), potassium persulfate $( \mathrm { K } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 8 } )$ , formic acid, acetonitrile, 2, 2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH), 2, 2-azino-bis (3-ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulfonic acid) diammonium salt (ABTS), and amino acid standard (AAS18) were obtained from Sigma Chemicals Co. (USA). All other chemical reagents were of analytical grade purity and obtained from Peking Chemical Plant (Beijing, China).

# 3.2. Preparation of Gelatin Peptides with Different MWs

Gelatin peptides were prepared according to the method of Yu et al. [35]. Briefly, 5 g of donkey-hide gelatin was dissolved in 120 mL of water and then simmered in a water bath at $8 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 30 min. After cooling at $6 3 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ , the pH of the donkey-hide gelatin solution was adjusted to 10.5 using NaOH (1 mol/L), and Alcalase 2.4L (enzyme to substrate ratio of $9 \% )$ was added to initiate hydrolysis. During enzymolysis, the pH range was maintained within ±0.05. After hydrolysis for 3 h, the enzyme was inactivated in a water bath at $9 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 10 min, followed by centrifugation of gelatin hydrolysates for 10 min at $1 0 ^ { 4 }$ r/min and $4 ^ { \circ } C .$ . Then, the supernatant was filtered through Amicon ultra centrifugal filters (Millipore, Burlington, MA, USA) with interceptions of 30, 10, 3, and 1 kDa. Finally, the gelatin-derived peptide solutions with different MWs were obtained.

# 3.3. Analysis of the Amino Acid Composition of Gelatin Peptides

Overall, 100 mg of gelatin peptide powder was placed in a hydrolytic tube, and 10 mL of HCl (6 M) was added to the tube in a ratio of 1:1. Nitrogen was blown into the tube for ${ 3 0 \ } \mathbf { s } ,$ after which the tube was sealed. Then, the sample was hydrolyzed in an oil bath at $1 1 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 24 h. After hydrolysis, it was cooled to room temperature and filtered through a 0.45-µm membrane into a 50-mL volumetric bottle. Next, the samples were deacidified and filtered through a 0.45-µm filter for machine analysis using Biochrom 30+ amino acid analyzer (Biochrom Ltd., FCE, Cambridge, UK). An Na-type cationic resin chromatography column (200 mm × 4.6 mm) was used for gradient elution. The temperature of the separation column was $5 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } \mathrm { - } 6 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } \mathrm { - } 7 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , and the temperature of the reaction tank was $1 3 8 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ . The flow rate of the buffer solution was 20 mL $, / \mathrm { h } ,$ whereas that of the reaction solution was 10 mL/h. The sample volume was $5 0 \mu \mathrm { L } ,$ , and the ultraviolet (UV) detection wavelengths were 570 nm and 440 nm.

# 3.4. Analysis of the Functional Groups of Gelatin Peptides via FTIR Spectroscopy

FTIR spectroscopy was performed with a resolution of 4 $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ over the range of $4 0 0 0 { - } 4 0 0 ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ using a UV spectrometer (Thermo Nicolet iS5, Thermo Fisher, Waltham, MA, USA). Briefly, 2 mg of peptide powder and 200 mg of dried KBr were mixed to prepare the sample pellets. The pellets were placed in a sample compartment and measured 32 times at a scanning speed of 2.8 mm/s. After background correction (dried KBr spectrum used as background), the sample spectra were obtained.

# 3.5. Analysis of the Secondary Structure of Gelatin Peptides via CD

The CD spectra and secondary structures were analyzed using Chirascan 100 Circular Dichroism Spectropolarimeter (Applied Photophysics Ltd., FCE, Surrey, UK). Before the detection test, the nitrogen flow rate was adjusted to between 0.15 and 0.2 MPa; nitrogen was passed for 30 min, and the gas in the optical path of the instrument was removed. The gelatin peptide powder was mixed with deionized water to form a liquid sample (1 mg/mL), which was then slowly poured into the sample pool with an optical path of 1.0 cm for the test. The wavelength range was set from 190 to 270 nm; optimal bandwidth

was set to 1 nm; scanning speed was set to 100 nm/min; and the scan time was set to three accumulations. Finally, the data were analyzed using the following equation [36]:

$$
[ \theta ] = \frac {\theta}{1 0 L C N}
$$

where θ indicates instrument readings, L indicates the path length (cm), C indicates concentration of the peptide (mol/L), and N indicates the number of amino acid residues in the peptide.

# 3.6. Determination of the Antioxidant Activity of Gelatin Peptides

# 3.6.1. DPPH Radical Scavenging Assay of Gelatin Peptides

The reaction system comprised of 96-well microplates containing 100 µL of gelatin peptide solution (6 mg/mL), 100 µL of fresh DPPH (0.6 mM), and 100 µL of methanol. Subsequently, samples were shaken vigorously and incubated at 25 ◦C for 30 min under dark conditions. Then, the absorbance was measured at a wavelength of 515 nm (using methanol as a blank). Finally, the DPPH radical scavenging activity of gelatin peptides was estimated using the following equation:

$$
\mathrm{DPPH}\text{radical}\text{scavening activity} (\%) = (1 - \frac{\text{Asample}}{\text{Ablank}})\times 100
$$

# 3.6.2. ABTS Radical Scavenging Assay of Gelatin Peptides

The ABTS radical scavenging assay was performed in accordance with the method of Kozics et al. with minor modifications [37]. Overall, 10 mL of ABTS (7 mM) and 10 mL of ${ \mathrm { K } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { S } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 8 }$ (2.45 mM) were mixed under dark conditions for 16 h to generate ABTS radical cations. Then, 50 µL of gelatin peptide solution (6 mg/mL) or deionized water (as blank) was added to 150 µL of diluted ABTS solution (absorbance of $0 . 7 0 \pm 0 . 0 2$ at 734 nm) in a 96-well microplate. Subsequently, the solution was left to incubate for 6 min under dark conditions, and the absorbance was measured at a wavelength of 734 nm. The ABTS scavenging activity of gelatin peptides with different MWs was calculated as follows:

$$
\text{ABTS radical scavenging activity} (\%) = (1 - \frac{\text{Asample}}{\text{Ablank}})\times 100
$$

# 3.7. Peptide Sequence Identification Using Liquid Chromatography (LC)–Tandem Mass Spectrometry (MS/MS)

A Zorbax 300SB-C18 peptide trap (Agilent Technologies, Wilmington, DE, USA) was used to separate the gelatin peptides, and while a RP-C18 capillary column was used as the analytical column (0.15 mm × 150 mm; Column Technology Inc., Mississippi, USA). Separation was performed using a mobile phase consisting of 0.1% (v/v) formic acid aqueous solution (A) and 0.1% (v/v) formic acid acetonitrile solution (B), according to the method of Yu et al. [38]. The elution conditions were set as follows: 0–50 min, 4% B → 50% B; 50–54 min, 50% B → 100% B; and 54–60 min, 100% B. After the separation of gelatin peptides via capillary high-performance LC, they were analyzed via MS using a Q Exactive mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher, Mass, USA). The analysis duration was set to 60 min, and detection was performed in the positive-ion mode. Ten fragment maps (MS2 scan) were collected after each full scan. Finally, the raw mass spectrum file was uploaded to MaxQuant 1.5.5.1 to obtain peptide sequences based on the database UniProt_Equus_asinus_33662_20221212. The peptide tolerance was set to 20 ppm, MS/MS tolerance was set to 0.1 Da, and false discovery rate of peptides and proteins was set to ≤0.01.

# 3.8. Peptide Synthesis

The antioxidant peptides with known sequences were synthesized by Hubei Qiangyao Biotech Co., Ltd. (Hubei, China), using Fmoc-protected amino acid synthesis.

# 3.9. Antioxidant Activity Tests of Synthetic Peptides

The antioxidant activity of synthetic peptides was tested using DPPH and ABTS radical scavenging assays, as described in Section 2.6. The concentration of synthetic peptides was determined to be 2 and 1 mg/mL according to DPPH and ABTS assays, respectively.

# 3.10. Molecular Docking of Gelatin Peptides with Keap1

The Keap1 protein with a three-dimensional crystal structure (obtained by ab initio modeling with AlphaFold2 [39]) was used as the initial receptor for molecular docking, and the PGPAP polypeptide was a straight chain structure directly constructed via Pymol [40]. The random coil part (1–55 amino acid residues) with very low modeling quality was deleted in the Keap1 sequence. This structure section is far from the overall active structure of the protein and has no impact on the biological function of the whole protein. The polypeptide and Keap1 were connected globally, and the sites with the strongest binding effect were selected for analysis. The binding site of the polypeptide molecule in a protein is primarily located in the cavity above the center of the barrel structure, which is composed of a large number of β-sheets at the C-terminus of the protein. Therefore, the active docking site of the polypeptide and protein was selected in this pocket. Molecular docking was implemented using AutoDock 4.2.6, and the center coordinates of the docking box were set as follows: x = 14.219, y = 1.850, and $z = - 2 1 . 6 1 3 .$ . The number of cells in each XYZ direction was set to $6 0 \times 6 0 \times 6 0$ , and the frequency of docking was set to 100 times. The docking was carried out by Lamarckian genetic algorithm in Autodock. The whole docking process adopted a semi-flexible method; that is, the receptor was regarded as rigid and the ligand as flexible. An independent docking run was performed during the molecular docking of gelatin peptides with Keap1. In this docking run, the protein and the small molecule were docked 50 times. An Amber14 force field was adopted for energy optimization [30]. It was carried out in two steps: firstly, the structure was optimized by the steepest descent method with 1000 steps, and then further optimized by the conjugate gradient method with 500 steps.

# 3.11. Molecular Dynamic (MD) Simulations of the PGPAP-Keap1 Complex

Gromacs 2018.4 [30] was used to run MD simulations of the PGPAP-Keap1 complex using the Amber14SB force field [41] and TIP3P water model [30]. During MD simulation, all bonds involving hydrogen atoms were constrained using the LINCS algorithm, and the integral step was 2 fsc. The electrostatic interaction was calculated using the particlemesh Ewald method. The nonbond interaction cutoff value was set to 10 Å and was updated every 10 steps. The simulated temperature was controlled at 298.15 K using the V-rescale temperature coupling method, and the pressure was controlled at 1 bar using the Parrinello–Rahman method.

# 3.12. Statistical Analysis

One-way analysis of variance was used to perform triplicate analyses using SPSS 13.0 software (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). All data were presented as the mean ± standard. A p-value of < 0.05 was considered to indicate statistical significance.

# 4. Conclusions

This study investigated the structural characteristics and antioxidant mechanism of donkey-hide gelatin peptides. The DPPH and ABTS free radical scavenging activity assays indicated that gelatin peptides with a MW of 1–3 kDa had the strongest antioxidant activity. Amino acid analysis, FTIR spectroscopy, and CD revealed that gelatin peptides with different MWs differed in terms of amino acid composition, peak strength of functional groups, and content of secondary structures, which might result in different antioxidant activities. In addition, molecular docking and MD simulation indicated that PGPAP could bind to the Keap1 protein at the following key residues: Arg415, Gly462, Phe478, and Tyr572. The PGPAP–Keap1 complex exhibited stable and compact conformations, which

appear a plausible basis to exert its biological function. Overall, the antioxidant activity of gelatin peptides is closely related to their structural properties, and PGPAP may serve as an antioxidant peptide targeting in vivo metabolism.

# Ejiao peptide-iron chelates regulate the metabolism of iron deficiency anemia mice and improve the bioavailability of iron

![](images/ea178a49cbf3a69243d6595cf708992349d1d0c7b51bcda6d121366b6004e6ea.jpg)

Xiang-Rong Cheng a,b,* , Yu-Yao Chen a,b , Cong-Cong Cao a,b , Jia-Hui Ma a,b , Chen-Xi Zhang a,b , Zi-Wei Zhao a,b , Qian Wu b,c , Yuan-Yuan Li c , Mitchell N. Muskat d , Guo-Qing Wu a,e,**

a State Key Laboratory of Food Science and Resources, Jiangnan University, Wuxi, 214122, China   
b School of Food Science and Technology, Jiangnan University, Wuxi, 214122, China   
c NHC Key Lab of Reproduction Regulation (Shanghai Institute for Biomedical and Pharmaceutical Technologies), Fudan University, Shanghai, 200080, China   
d School of Pharmacy, University of California San Francisco, San Francisco, CA, 94143, USA   
e School of Public Health, Health Science Center, Ningbo University, Zhejiang, 315211, China

# A R T I C L E I N F O

Keywords:

Colla Corii Asini

Hematopoietic activity

Iron homeostasis

Metabolomics

Peptide-iron chelates

# A B S T R A C T

Colla Corii Asini (Ejiao) peptide-iron (EPI) chelates formed during digestion have been revealed as potential hematopoietic components. However, it remains unclear how EPI regulates endogenous metabolism in vivo. Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) mice were gavaged with EPI chelates in a gradient dosage, while Ejiao hydrolysate-iron (EJI) chelates and FeSO4 were used as positive controls. The effect of EPI on hematopoietic recovery was evaluated. For the plasma untargeted metabolomic analysis, liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) were applied to identify metabolites in the samples. EPI significantly increased the levels of hemogram in IDA mice in a dose-dependent manner. The relative iron bioavailability in EPI was 123.45% of that in FeSO in vivo. After high dose of EPI (EPI-H) supplementation, the levels of 22 potential metabolic markers in the IDA group returned to normal, including sphingomyelin and arachidonic acid. EPI-H affected endogenous metabolites by regulating the metabolism of energy, lipids, and amino acids, promoted hematopoiesis, regulated metabolic pathways, and improved iron homeostasis. It’s a comprehensive nutritional intervention of IDA by EPI supplementation.

# 1. Introduction

Iron is of crucial importance in influencing human cell proliferation and energy metabolism. Meanwhile, it is also a fundamental element for hemoglobin, myoglobin, and cytochromes (Ganz, 2018; Walters et al., 2018).Long-term iron deficiency causes the consumption of iron stores from the body, which eventually leads to iron deficiency anemia (IDA). In turn, IDA affects the nervous and immune systems (Bouri & Martin, 2018; Hassan et al., 2016; Yokusoglu et al., 2007). IDA has been widely distributed across the world with a significantly higher proportion in developing countries than that in developed countries, causing costs with marked implications for the economic development (Schümann et al., 2007).

Iron supplementation can effectively intervene and treat iron deficiency and related diseases (Al Hassan, 2015). In general, oral iron is the main interventional treatment for IDA (Qi et al., 2020). Oral iron has

developed from inorganic ferrous salts and organic acid salts to macromolecular iron chelates to date. The macromolecular iron chelates are transported via specific receptors in the intestinal cells, improving the tolerability and bioavailability of iron (Cancelo-Hidalgo et al., 2013; YLiu et al., 2018; Nappi et al., 2009). Peptide-iron chelate promotes the transport and absorption of iron in the body, significantly alleviating IDA symptoms (Walters et al., 2018). Recent researches have described that peptides from different sources chelate with iron to form bioactive iron chelates, such as Alaska pollock skin (Guo et al., 2013), scad (Jiang et al., 2019), anchovies (Wu et al., 2012), etc. These studies described in detail the preparation methods of chelates and the ability of the body to absorb iron. However, there is a lack of research on the effects of peptide-iron chelate on the metabolism of the body. Moreover, iron deficiency or iron overload caused by improper absorption of iron supplements significantly affect the metabolic level of the body. The change of iron content affects the combination of transferrin to interfere

with erythropoiesis, and interferes with the uptake and utilization of iron by the liver, as well as other related metabolic pathways (Rishi & Subramaniam, 2017; Rishi et al., 2015). Therefore, it is necessary to study the changes of body metabolism caused by intake of iron supplements.

Colla Corii Asini (Ejiao) is both a traditional medicine and functional food in China. It is a gelatin-like preparation derived from processed donkey skin (Wang et al., 2014). Ejiao has been used for hematopoiesis in traditional Chinese medicine. It is used to treat anemia and related diseases for over 2000 years (Zhang et al., 2021). The main components of Ejiao are proteins/gelatins, polysaccharides, trace elements, dermatan sulfate, and biological acids (Wang et al., 2014). Studies have shown that Ejiao significantly improves anemia symptoms in β-thalassemia patients (Li et al., 2016), and promote the recovery of hematopoietic function in myelosuppressed mice (Liu et al., 2014).

The research of Li shows that the Ejiao peptide-iron (EPI) chelates can improve the hemogram index of iron deficiency anemia mice more effectively than the original solution of Ejiao (Li et al., 2019). This may be because the iron in the chelate plays a stronger role in hematopoiesis. Our research group has carried out some relevant studies on EPI chelates in recent years. A previous study showed that the hydrolysate of Ejiao has a high capacity to chelate iron during digestion, forming the Ejiao hydrolysate-iron (EJI) chelates, which may contribute to hematopoiesis. The EPI chelates derived from EJI chelates may have the potential to promote iron absorption and thus improved hematopoiesis, but the specific hematopoiesis mechanism needs further study (Cao et al., 2021). In dietary iron deficiency mice, EPI chelates treatment inhibited the intestinal inflammation, and increased microbial diversity and richness to alleviate microbiota dysbiosis caused by IDA (Cheng et al., 2021). Iron homeostasis and the related metabolic pathways interact with intestinal flora, so changes in intestinal flora caused by EPI will also cause variations in body metabolism. However, it remains unclear how EPI regulates metabolism in vivo. This research evaluated the hematopoietic effects and metabolic regulation of EPI in dietary IDA mice and the underlying mechanism. This work would help to understand the ability of EPI chelates to improve hematopoiesis and their regulatory effects on metabolism, promoting the development and application of EPI chelates.

# 2. Materials and methods

# 2.1. Materials and reagents

Ejiao powder was purchased from Dong-E-E-Jiao $\mathbf { \boldsymbol { C 0 } } .$ , Ltd. (Shandong, China). Pepsin (≥ 2500 U/mg) was purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Trypsin (≥ 50 U/ mg), phenanthroline, FeSO and other reagents were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China).

# 2.2. Animals and treatments

All experiments in this study were conducted in accordance with the European Community guidelines (directive 2010/63/EU) for the care and use of experimental animals. The study design was approved by the Ethics Committee of Jiangnan University, China (JN. no. 20190930i0881220 [239]).

3-week-old male ICR mice (Shanghai Laboratory Animal $\mathrm { C o . , }$ , Shanghai, China) were housed in a standardization specific pathogenfree (SPF) animal laboratory with access to food and water ad libitum. Iron contamination was avoided during the process of feeding. After 1 week of acclimation, animals were randomly divided into 11 groups (8 mice each). The mice were fed with either standard diet or low-iron diet which were purchased from Trophic Animal Feed High-tech Co. Ltd (Jiangsu, China). The control group (CON) was fed with diet containing Fe of 45 mg ${ \bf k } { \bf g } ^ { - 1 }$ . Other 10 groups were fed with low-iron diet containing Fe of 12 mg $\mathbf { k } \mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ . It is considered that dietary IDA has been induced

successfully for low-iron diet feeding when the hemoglobin (HGB) content in mice was less than 90 $g \mathrm { L } ^ { - 1 }$ (Song et al., 2016). After 4 weeks, the HGB content of mice fed with low iron-diet was 85. $6 7 \pm 3 . 0 4 \ \mathrm { g \ L ^ { - 1 } } ,$ , while that of normal mice was $1 5 8 . 5 7 \pm 9 . 0 7 \mathrm { ~ g ~ L } ^ { - 1 }$ 1, indicating that dietary iron deficiency anemia had been successfully induced.

After iron depletion, 10 groups of IDA mice were further gavaged with saline (IDA group), low, medium, and high doses (1.0, 2.0, and 3.0 mg Fe per kg weight, respectively) of EPI solution (EPI-L, EPI-M, EPI-H groups), $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ solution $\mathrm { ( F e S O _ { 4 } \mathrm { - L } }$ , $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 } – \mathrm { M } ,$ , $\mathrm { F e S O _ { 4 } \mathrm { - H } }$ groups), and EJI solution $\mathrm { ( E J I - L , }$ EJI-M, EJI-H groups). These groups mice were continuously intervened for 4 weeks. The gradient dosage of the intervention agent refers to the experiments of Cheng and Song (Cheng et al., 2021; Song et al., 2016). Considering that $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ is one of the main raw materials of EPI chelates and has a certain contribution to the recovery of IDA, $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ gavage was set as positive control for the comparison of intervention effect between $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ and EPI chelates on IDA (Cheng et al., 2021). Since EPI chelates were prepared from EJI chelates, the EJI groups were also set as positive controls, so as to clarify the functional similarity and difference between EPI chelates and EJI chelates.

Mouse body weights were weekly measured during the experimental period. Weight growth rate was calculated by the ratio of body weight increase after 4 weeks of iron supplementation to the initial body weight before iron supplementation. Blood samples were collected at the end of the feeding period from the retro-orbital venous plexus after anesthetization. Serum was obtained by centrifugation for 15 min at 4000 rpm; whole blood was collected into tubes containing heparin and the plasma was obtained by centrifugation for 15 min at 3000 rpm. Mice were euthanized by cervical dislocation, the heart, spleen, and liver were weighed. All samples were stored at ${ } ^ { - 8 0 } { } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ until analysis.

# 2.3. Preparation of EPI and EJI

EJI and EPI were prepared as previously reported (Cao et al., 2021). In brief, Ejiao powder was hydrolyzed by digestive enzymes. The Ejiao hydrolysate was further purified by immobilized metal affinity chromatography to afford Ejiao peptides with iron chelating capability. Finally, the Ejiao hydrolysate and Ejiao peptides were chelated with $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ to yield Ejiao hydrolysate-iron and Ejiao peptide-iron chelates, respectively.

# 2.4. Determination of hemogram indices

Hematological tests were performed with an automatic hematology analyzer (sysmex XT-2000i, Sysmex Corporation, Japan). The hemogram indices included HGB, red blood cells (RBC), hematocrit (HCT), mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH), mean corpuscular volume (MCV), and mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC) were analyzed.

# 2.5. Calculation of relative iron bioavailability of supplements

The relative iron bioavailability was determined by a hemoglobin repletion/slope ratio method, a standard calculation method recommended by the Association of Official Analytical Chemists (AOAC) (Swain et $\mathrm { a l . , }$ 2003). Linear regression equation between the increase of HGB and the dose of iron supplement was established for different iron supplements. The slopes represented the iron bioavailability of supplements, while the slope ratio between EJI or EPI and $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ (Eq. (1)) represented their relative bioavailability respectively (Lin et al., 2019).

$$
\text{Relative iron bioavailability} (\%) = \frac {\text {Equation slope of iron supplements}}{\text {Equation slope of FeSO} _ {4}} \times 100 \tag{1}
$$

# 2.6. Determination of iron homeostasis

The serum iron (SI), serum ferritin (SF), unsaturated iron binding capacity (UIBC), transferrin (TRF), and hepcidin (Hepc) were determined using commercial ELISA kits (Huijia Biotechnology Co., Ltd, Fujian, China) following the manufacturers’ instructions. These kits used the double-antibody sandwich enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay to determine the concentration of antibody above. Use the Microplate Reader 96 to measure the absorbance (OD value) at 450 nm wavelength, and then the antibody concentration in the sample were calculated.

# 2.7. Determination of iron content in tissues

50–100 mg of freeze-dried tissue was transferred to a Teflon digestion tank and mixed with 5 mL of concentrated nitric acid for microwave digestion. This process was performed according to the digestion procedure in Table S1 to obtain a clear solution. The liver and spleen of mice were analyzed for iron content by atomic absorption spectroscopy (AA 240 atomic absorption spectrometer, Varian, USA)(Suliburska et al., 2021).

# 2.8. Histological analysis

The fresh liver tissue was fixed with 4% of paraformaldehyde solution, embedded in paraffin, cut into 5 μm sections, and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E). The slices were visualized under an optical microscope (Olympus, Tokyo, Japan) with 200 magnifications (Huan He et al., 2018).

# 2.9. Untargeted metabolomics analysis for plasma based on LC-MS/MS

The metabolomics analysis and data pre-processing were conducted following the previous procedure (S. A. Qi et al., 2021). In brief, each defrosted plasma (100 μL) was mixed with 300 μL of 80% methanol, vortexed for $^ { 3 0 \ s , }$ stood for 1 h $\mathrm { a t - } 2 0 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ and then centrifuged twice at 12, 000 rpm at $4 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 15 min. The obtained supernatant $( 2 0 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { L } )$ was adopted for the reversed-phase liquid chromatography (RPLC)-MS analysis. The 2-chloro-L-phenylalanine and lysophosphatidylcholine 12:0 were used as internal standards. An Ultimate-3000 UPLC system coupled to a Q Exactive hybrid quadrupole-Orbitrap mass spectrometry

system (Thermo Scientific) was used for the sample analysis. Untargeted metabolomic analysis was performed by RPLC-MS with $\mathrm { E } { \mathsf { S } } \mathrm { I } ^ { + }$ and ESI− mode. MS raw data were acquired using the software Xcalibur (version 3.1, Thermo Scientific), and a workflow named “Untargeted Metabolomics with statistics detect unknowns with ID using Online Database and mzLogic” was selected for processing. The normalized dataset was imported into SIMCA (V15.0, Umetrics, Umeå, Sweden) for further multivariate statistical analysis.

# 2.10. Statistical analysis

Statistical analysis was performed using the software package SPSS version 23.0. Results were presented as mean ± SEM. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), followed by the Duncan’s multiple comparison test was used for comparison among multiple groups with the significance level taken at $p < 0 . 0 5$ .

# 3. Results

# 3.1. Hematopoietic function of EPI

As shown in Fig. 1, the IDA model mice, compared with CON group, had a significant reduction of body weight and weight growth rate, and notable increase of the indices of heart, liver, and spleen (Fig. 1A–E). The results of these indices of organs were similar with those observed by Xiao et al. (Xiao et al., 2016). Moreover, mice treated with the EPI, EJI or $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ had higher $( p < 0 . 0 5 )$ body weight (Fig. 1A) and weight growth rate (Fig. 1B) than those of the IDA mice. The indices of the heart, liver, and spleen of mice in iron supplemented groups were significantly lower $( p < 0 . 0 5 )$ than those in the IDA group (Fig. 1C–E). It’s worth noting that the high dose of three iron supplements ameliorated the IDA more significantly than other groups, indicating that the EPI, EJI and $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ recovery IDA in a dose-dependent manner. Particularly, the high-dose EPI and EJI, rather than $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ intervention normalized the organ index of IDA mice to the level of CON mice $( p <$ 0.05).

The level of hemogram index reflects the ability of hematopoiesis. The blood indicators in each group are shown in Table 1. HGB, RBC, HCT, MCV, MCH, and MCHC values in the IDA group were significantly lower than those in the CON group $( p < 0 . 0 5 )$ . Collectively, the changes of weight, weight growth rate, organ index and hematologic parameters of mice show the effect of EPI, EJI, and $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ on hematopoietic improvement in a dose-dependent manner in IDA mice. Moreover, the different dose of EJI and EPI intervention

improved more effective hematopoietic function than that of corresponding $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ groups. The indexes of hematopoietic function of the high-dose EJI and EPI intervention were significantly enhanced, almost up to the CON level.

# 3.2. The effects of EPI on the liver histological changes induced by IDA

The liver acts as the central regulator of iron homeostasis, and the hepcidin produced by it is intimately involved in the process of erythropoiesis (Rishi & Subramaniam, 2017; Rishi et al., 2015). It is necessary to observe the changes of liver tissue structure due to different types of iron intake during the treatment period. Liver tissue sections of CON, IDA and three high-dose treatment groups $( \mathrm { F e S O _ { 4 } \mathrm { - } H , \mathrm { E P I \mathrm { - } H , \mathrm { E J I \mathrm { - } H ) } } }$ were stained with H&E to investigate the beneficial function of EPI on the hepatic sinusoids of IDA mice (Fig. 2). The histopathological examination of liver sections from the CON mice showed complete structure of hepatic lobules with hepatic blood sinuses arranged as cords radiating from the central vein. The boundary of hepatic cord was clear, and the nucleus of hepatocytes was obvious. On the contrary, in the IDA group, the hepatic sinuses around the central vein are disordered and dilated, with the indistinct hepatocellular cord. In the three high-dose groups, all three iron supplements reduced the deterioration of liver tissue morphology to a certain extent. With the treatment of high dose of EPI or EJI, the architecture of hepatic lobules was ameliorated to normal level, and the disordered arrangement of hepatic sinusoids resulted from IDA was improved; while the hepatic sinuses of mice in the $\mathrm { F e S O _ { 4 } \mathrm { - H } }$ group was still disordered, and the boundary of hepatic cord was not clear enough. These results indicated that with high-dose iron supplementation, the disorder of hepatic sinusoids was improved to varying degrees, and the effect of supplementing EPI and EJI on repairing the state of liver tissue was better than that of $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ intervention.

# 3.3. EPI improves the absorption and regulation of iron in IDA mice

# 3.3.1. Relative iron bioavailability

As shown in Table $^ { 2 , }$ the HGB content of IDA mice was less than 90 $\mathbf { g } { \cdot } \mathbf { L } ^ { - 1 }$ after four weeks iron depletion. The supplementation of either EPI, EJI, or $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ distinctly increased the HGB contents. Taking $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ as the reference standard, the relative iron bioavailability in EPI and EJI groups were 123.45% and 117.70%, respectively. These results

suggested that the chelated iron in EPI and EJI had higher iron bioavailability than the free iron in $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 } .$ . Because the proportion of components with high iron chelating capacity is larger in EPI, EPI has higher chelating strength. Zhang et al. showed that the relative bioavailability of organic Fe sources was related to the chelation strength, and the organic Fe sources with greater chelation strength showed higher iron bioavailability (Zhang, Lu, et al., 2016). This explains why the bioavailability of EPI group is higher than that of EJI group. $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ is absorbed in the intestine as ferrous ions, and the different transport pathway with iron chelates may have contributed to the lowest bioavailability of $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ .

# 3.3.2. Effect of EPI on iron homeostasis in IDA mice

To explain the changes of iron status in mice, we detected levels of indices related to the regulation of iron homeostasis (Fig. 3A–F). Compared with CON group, the levels of serum iron (Fig. 3A), serum ferritin (Fig. 3B), serum hepcidin (Fig. 3E) and hepatic hepcidin (Fig. 3F) in the IDA group were significantly declined, and UIBC and TRF levels were significantly decreased $( p < 0 . 0 5 )$ . However, compared to IDA group, these indexes were significantly reversed by iron supplements in different dose EPI and EJI groups, $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 } – \mathbf { M }$ and $\mathrm { F e S O _ { 4 } \mathrm { - H } } .$ . Even these six indices in the EPI-H and EJI-H groups returned to the normal levels. Besides, high dose of EPI or EJI notably increased the iron content of liver and spleen, up to normal levels $( p < 0 . 0 5 ,$ Fig. 3G and H). The change of iron content in the organ and the levels of indices related to the regulation of iron homeostasis reflects the changes of iron homeostasis. Dose-dependent effect were found in EPI, EJI and $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ groups, respectively (Fig. 3). These data show that EPI and EJI treatment effectively regulate the iron homeostasis, while the $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ performed poorly. There exists dose-dependent effect in all EPI, EJI and $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ groups. The consistency in the functions of EPI chelates and EJI chelates in regulating iron homeostasis illustrates their structural similarities, which provides support for the demonstration that EPI is a major functional component of EJI.

# 3.4. Metabolic regulation of EPI on IDA mice

# 3.4.1. Multivariate statistical analysis of plasma metabolic data

Multivariate statistical analysis was performed on the positive and negative ion mode data from plasma samples of the CON, IDA, and highdose administration groups to obtain the PCA and OPLS-DA score plot (Fig. 4). The distribution of plasma samples in the PCA score plot didn’t indicate a separation among the CON group and high-dose administration groups. The supervised OPLS-DA score plot showed obvious separation of the CON group, IDA group and high-dose administration groups in both positive and negative ion modes. Among the three treatment groups, the $\mathrm { F e S O _ { 4 } { - } H }$ group was separated from the EJI-H group and the EPI-H group obviously. These data indicate that the dietary-induced iron deficiency anemia changes the plasma metabolic characteristics of normal mice. The treatment of three iron supplements improved the IDA differently. EPI and EJI may improve IDA through similar ways, because of the similarity of LC-MS data of plasma

metabolites in the two groups.

The OPLS-DA score plot and $( \nabla + \mathbf { S } )$ -plot of plasma sample metabolic data in both positive ion mode (Fig. 5) and negative ion mode (Fig. 6) help to screen the differential metabolites of IDA, and also explain the changes of plasma metabolites in IDA mice after treatment with different iron supplements. (V + S)-plot reflects the correlation between metabolites and models. The screening of differential metabolites is based on two indicators: p (corr) (correlation coefficient) and VIP (variable importance in the projection). In the $\mathrm { ( V + \thinspace S ) { \ - } p l o t } .$ , variables that meet the two conditions of VIP value > 1, absolute value of $\mathsf { p } \left( \mathsf { c o r r } \right) > 0 . 6$ are considered as potential biomarkers. The farther the variable is from the origin, the greater contribution is considered to the difference between the two groups. It helps to identify metabolites with statistical significance and potential biochemical significance according to their contribution and reliability to the model (Wiklund et al., 2008). The IDA group was significantly separated from the CON group, indicating that the IDA was successfully induced (Figs. 5A and 6A). The EPI group was significantly separated from the IDA group (Figs. 5C and 6C), indicating that EPI may improve the hematopoietic activity of IDA mice by change the plasma endogenous metabolites. The EPI and $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ groups are also completely separated (Figs. 5E and 6E), indicating that there may be differences in the activation pathway of EPI and $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ to improve IDA. In addition, the EPI and EJI groups were obviously separated (Figs. S1 and S2), indicating a few differences in metabolic regulation in IDA mice after EPI and EJI supplementation.

# 3.4.2. Screening and identification of plasma differential metabolites

The identified metabolites were compared with the Human Metabolome Database (HMDB). Twenty-two differential metabolites were identified in both positive and negative ion modes (Fig. 7). These metabolites were identified as potential metabolic markers of IDA. Compared to CON group, IDA group had a significant decline in the level of biliverdin, sphingomyelin, lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC), arachidonic acid, phenyl acetyl glycine, Methyl-3-iodoacetate and spermidine $( p < 0 . 0 1 )$ , while an obvious rise in the level of phosphatidylcholine, linoleic acid, dihydrosphingosine (DHS) and propionyl carnitine (p < 0.01, Fig. 7A) in positive ion mode. In addition, under the negative ion mode, methyl-acetoacetic acid, and eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) levels in the IDA group significantly decreased $( p < 0 . 0 1 )$ , while 4-phenol sulfonic acid, citric acid, 2-oxobutyric acid, 6-hydroxy caproic acid, succinic acid, lactic acid, pyruvic acid, cholic acid levels significantly increased $( p < 0 . 0 1$ , Fig. 7B). However, after iron supplementation especially EPI intervention, most potential metabolic markers affected by IDA returned to normal levels (Fig. 7) .

To illustrate the differences in metabolic regulation of IDA mice by EPI chelates and $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 } ,$ we further investigated which characteristic differential metabolic markers were identified in the EPI group compared with the IDA and $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ groups, respectively. Compared with the IDA group, thirty-five differential metabolic markers were regulated in the EPI group (Table S3 and Table S4). EPI significantly decreased the levels of L-proline, uracil, 4-hydroxybenzaldehyde, acetyl L-carnitine, Lmethionine, L-isoleucine, keto-leucine, oleic acid, oleic acid amide,

Kyoto encyclopedia of genes and genomes (KEGG) database was used to conduct metabolic pathway analysis of screened differential metabolic markers (Fig. 8). The influence value of potential metabolic pathway should be greater than 0.10. It’s found that both EPI and $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ were effectively involved in the regulation of the tricarboxylic acid cycle and arachidonic acid metabolic pathway. EPI additionally regulated histidine metabolism, pyruvate metabolism, glycolysis and gluconeogenesis, as well as cysteine and methionine metabolism, which may be one of the reasons why EPI had a more comprehensive intervention effect than $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 } .$ . This indicated that EPI regulated more metabolic pathways in vivo to improve the IDA better. These results collectively suggested that $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ was involved in regulating a few metabolism pathways to promote the improvement of IDA, while EPI was involved in more metabolic regulation pathways in energy metabolism, lipid metabolism and amino acid metabolism to achieve better IDA improvement effect. It is worth noting that the main metabolic pathways involved in the intervention of IDA by EPI and EJI were basically the same, except that EJI particularly regulated the biosynthesis of phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan, while EPI regulated histidine metabolism (Fig. 8A, C).

# 4. Discussion

Studies have proved that Ejiao can increase red blood cells and hemoglobin in the blood, and has an obvious therapeutic effect on IDA. Our previous studies have shown that EPI produced by simulated digestion has the potential to promote iron absorption, improve intestinal inflammation and protect intestinal flora. In this study, we verified the hematopoietic effect and the ability of EPI to promote iron absorp tion, and reported the mechanism of metabolic regulation of EPI on IDA mice.

The change in body weight reflects the growth state of the body. IDA mice are depressed and lose weight because the body does not absorb enough nutrients. The change in organ index can reflect the visceral lesions of animals and is an important indicator to evaluate the safety of drugs (Zhang, Lu, et al., 2016). IDA mice have significant changes in organ index, indicating that iron deficiency will affect the health level of organs, activate the compensatory mechanism of the body, and lead to organ hypertrophy (Xiao et al., 2016). The different degrees of decrease in organ index with different iron supplements illustrate that iron supplementation helps to restore organ damage caused by IDA, and that EPI chelates are more beneficial for the recovery of various organs in IDA

mice due to the high relative iron bioavailability. Hemogram indicators can directly reflect whether the body is anemic. HGB and RBC are important indicators for the diagnosis of IDA, reflecting the hemoglobinization of red blood cells (van Santen et al., 2011). EPI significantly improves the body indicators of IDA mice, and the improvement effect is significantly better than $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 } ,$ showing a relatively excellent hematopoietic capacity. It is worth noting that the improvement effect of each intervention group on IDA mice is dose-dependent, which provides theoretical support for the follow-up related to food and drug research and development.

Iron is widely distributed in the human body, with the highest content in the liver and spleen (Cediel et al., 2012). When IDA occurs, the SI level decreases, which means the level of iron element that can bind to transferrin decreases, so that UIBC level increases. Under normal circumstances, there is a positive correlation between SF content and iron content stored in the body. When iron is deficient, SF level will decrease (Bailey et al., 2015). Iron ions entering the blood must bind with TRF before they can be transported to the blood and synthesize HGB. Detecting the concentration of TRF has diagnostic value for evaluating IDA (Ahmad et al., 2019). Hepc regulates the dynamic balance of iron in the body and ensures the normal physiological function of the body (Agarwal, 2021). The change of gene expression levels related to iron homeostasis regulation indicate that high dose of EPI and EJI significantly regulates iron homeostasis. Although iron is widely distributed in the human body, the bioavailability of iron is limited, which may be due to the low water solubility of inorganic iron in non-acidic microenvironment (Lund et al., 1998). In order to improve the absorption and utilization of ingested iron, intestinal microorganisms will synthesize free iron into small, high-affinity iron chelating compounds (Xiao et al., 2017). In the present study, using the hemoglobin repletion/slope ratio method to analyze the relative bioavailability of iron, it can be found that the relative bioavailability of iron of EPI relative to FeSO4 has reached 123.45%, which proves that the chelation of iron with Ejiao peptide can effectively improve the absorption availability of iron, and positively confirms the ability of EPI to promote iron absorption.

Combined with the performance of hematopoietic function and iron absorption, it can be found that the improvement effect of EPI groups on IDA symptoms is better than $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ groups, but similar to EJI positive control groups. The peptides of EPI were separated by immobilized metal affinity chromatography from Ejiao hydrolysates, but had enhanced iron chelating capacity (Cao et al., 2021). It makes sense that

the EPI chelates showed higher iron bioavailability than the EJI chelates. Taken the origin of EPI into consideration, the consistent regulation on hemogram indices and iron homeostasis of EPI and EJI in IDA mice further indicate that EPI is the main functional component of EJI.

Metabonomics is an important part of systems biology, which could be applied to evaluate the changes in metabolites at the overall level. This experimental supplement is helpful to study the mechanism of disease occurrence, intervention, and treatment. Through LC-MS/MS and pattern discriminant analysis, we identified the metabolites of $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ and EPI in vivo. In addition, we compared the metabolic pathways of EPI, EJI, and $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ intervention in IDA mice.

Citric acid, 2-oxobutyric acid, succinic acid, lactic acid, and pyruvate levels in the plasma of IDA mice were significantly increased compared with the CON group $( p < 0 . 0 5 , \ \mathrm { F i g . } \ 7 )$ . The metabolites above are important intermediates of the tricarboxylic acid cycle under aerobic conditions (Akram, 2014). Supplementation with $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ and EPI significantly reduced citric acid and 2-oxobutyric acid in the plasma of IDA mice $( p < 0 . 0 5 )$ , and EPI significantly decreased succinic acid, lactic

acid, pyruvate, and malic acid $( p < 0 . 0 5 )$ . Research shows that iron participates in the oxygen transport, tissue respiration process and the regulation of energy metabolism. Iron deficiency greatly reduces the ability of red blood cells to transport oxygen, leading to the dominance of anaerobic respiration and hindering energy metabolism (Tian et al., 2017). Therefore, supplementation of $\mathrm { F e S O } _ { 4 }$ and EPI under iron deficiency can increase the body’s iron intake, promote aerobic respiration, and effectively improve IDA through tricarboxylic acid cycle. The increase of lactic acid, the final product of glycolysis, is caused by the lack of blood oxygen and the increase of anaerobic metabolism. If lactic acid in plasma increases, glucose will be relatively reduced, resulting in insufficient energy, which also indicates that IDA causes the decline of energy metabolism. Pyruvate, the final product of the glycolysis pathway, is oxidized in mitochondria to produce acetyl coenzyme A and enter the tricarboxylic acid cycle. It also participates in the metabolic process of pyruvate together with lactic acid. In addition, malic acid can also participate in mitochondrial energy metabolism and is an important product of the tricarboxylic acid cycle and pyruvate metabolism
